text.p: A supranational legal system at European or world level is needed to combat multi-billion-dollar organised crime rings effectively, the man spearheading Italy's fight against the Mafia said on Thursday.
Giancarlo Caselli, the chief public prosecutor in Palermo, Sicily, told a European Parliament hearing that such a system should involve common agreed standards on defining crimes and sentences.

"Criminals move around internationally unhindered by customs or frontier barriers. They have already created a transnational area, where investigators are hindered by territorial competences," he said.
"Criminals pass borders without papers. Investigators have to make use of extradition treaties and international agreements.
"We have to work towards the aim of making a supranational criminal system. We need synergy, which would mean that we can get rid of the disparities between the different legal systems."

Caselli quoted figures supplied by the International Monetary Fund saying international organised crime was worth from $700 billion to $1 trillion a year. The money was skilfully channelled into the legal economy, often using tax breaks.
"We see that organised crime has become the largest industry in the world," he told the hearing organised by the assembly's Liberal Group.
Trafficking in drugs and arms were the biggest money spinners, followed by illegal trafficking in nuclear materials, toxic waste and people.

Caselli said bilateral and multilateral extradition treaties negotiated between different countries lacked enough substance to be effective. "Often these texts are very general and cannot be implemented in practice," he said.
International criminals skilfully made use of discrepancies in law between one country and another, often taking up local citizenship to avoid being extradited, he said.
"These discrepancies in legislation are things that are fully and efficiently exploited by criminals, who often thwart any possible success by the police," he said.
He also said that United Nations conventions defining crime were patchily implemented.
Caselli said the 15-nation European Union should move towards establishing a supranational legal system at its current intergovernmental review.
The bloc's attention has been thrust onto the problem of cross-border crime after the discovery of four murdered girls in Belgium highlighted international links in paedophilia and stolen cars.
